subject: maths
title: Chapter 8 · Test 1
summary: A 15-question test on Year 8 Chapter 8: samples and populations, comparing data sets, complementary events, Venn diagrams and two-way tables, and experimental probability.
body:
This test covers Chapter 8, Probability and statistics: samples and populations, comparing data sets, probability and complementary events, Venn diagrams and two-way tables, and experimental probability.

## How to do this test

- **Time:** about 25 minutes.
- **Conditions:** no notes and no calculator unless the question says. Show your working on paper.
- **Diagrams:** many questions have a graph, dot plot, spinner, grid or Venn diagram — read the numbers on it carefully.
- **Levels:** 4 easy, 5 medium, 4 hard and 2 challenge questions.
- **After marking:** for each question you got wrong, go back to the lesson it came from and redo its worked examples. Then try another Chapter 8 test — each one has different questions on the same skills.

questions.prompt: A Year 8 coordinator wants to know what Year 8 students at her school thought of camp. She asks every Year 8 student at the school to rate the camp. Is this a census or a sample?

options.A: A sample, because the students in other year levels were not asked
options.B: A sample, because a rating is an opinion, not a measurement
options.C: A census, because every member of the population (all Year 8 students at the school) was asked
options.D: Neither, because only the government can run a census

questions.explanation: The population is all Year 8 students at the school, and every one of them was asked, so it is a census. It is not a sample just because other year levels were left out — they are not in the population.
steps: Find the population: the group the question is about — all Year 8 students at the school.
Every member of that population was asked, so this is a census.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the population is only the Year 8 students at the school — the question is about them. Other year levels are not part of it.
mistakes.B: Step 2: whether it is a census depends on WHO is asked (all or part of the population), not on the type of data.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a census just means collecting data from every member of the population — anyone can run one.

questions.prompt: A school has 1200 students. The column graph shows the favourite sport of a random sample of 80 of them. Estimate how many students at the whole school have basketball as their favourite sport.
questions.explanation: The sample fraction is 22/80 = 0.275, and 0.275 × 1200 = 330. Giving 27.5 stops at the percentage of the sample — it still has to be applied to the 1200 students.
steps: Read the graph: 22 of the 80 students in the sample chose basketball.
Fraction of the sample: 22/80 = 0.275. Assume the whole school is the same, because the sample is random.
Estimate: 0.275 × 1200 = 330 students.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 22/80 = 27.5% is the percentage of the sample. Multiply the fraction by the 1200 students to get a number of students.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 22 is a count out of 80, not 22%. Use the fraction 22/80, not 22/100.
mistakes.D: Step 2: subtracting 22 from 1200 doesn’t estimate anything. Multiply the sample fraction by the school size.

questions.diagram_alt: Column graph for a sample of 80 students: football 28, netball 16, basketball 22, cricket 14

questions.prompt: The column graph shows the members of a swimming club by age group. A stratified sample of 40 members is chosen so that each age group is in the same proportion as in the club. How many members aged 12 to 17 should be in the sample?
questions.explanation: The 12 to 17 group is 270/600 = 0.45 of the club, so it gets 0.45 × 40 = 18 places in the sample. Sharing equally (about 13.3 each) ignores that this group is the biggest.
steps: Total members: 150 + 270 + 180 = 600.
Fraction aged 12 to 17: 270/600 = 0.45.
Members aged 12 to 17 in the sample: 0.45 × 40 = 18.

mistakes.B: Step 2: sharing the 40 equally between the 3 groups ignores their sizes. Each group’s share must match its fraction of the club.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 270/600 = 45% is the percentage of the club. Multiply the fraction by the sample size, 40.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 270 ÷ 40 divides the group by the sample size. Find the group’s fraction of the club (270/600) first.

questions.diagram_alt: Column graph of club members: under 12 has 150, 12 to 17 has 270, 18 and over has 180

questions.prompt: The parallel dot plots show the times (in seconds) of two runners, Mo and Sam, in six 100 m races. Which runner is more consistent?

options.A: Sam, because his range is larger
options.B: Sam, because he ran the fastest time (12 seconds)
options.C: Mo, because his median is higher
options.D: Mo, because his range (3 seconds) is smaller than Sam’s (7 seconds)

questions.explanation: Consistency is about spread: Mo’s range is 3 seconds and Sam’s is 7, so Mo is more consistent. Sam’s single fastest time doesn’t make him consistent.
steps: Ranges: Mo = 17 − 14 = 3 seconds; Sam = 19 − 12 = 7 seconds.
More consistent means less spread out, so the smaller range wins: Mo.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a larger range means MORE spread out, so less consistent. Choose the smaller range.
mistakes.B: Step 1: one fast race doesn’t show consistency. Compare the ranges, which measure spread.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the median measures the centre, not consistency — and both medians are 15.5 anyway. Compare the ranges.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of race times in seconds: Mo has dots at 14, 15, 15, 16, 16 and 17; Sam has dots at 12, 13, 15, 16, 18 and 19

questions.prompt:
Back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot of quiz scores (key: 2 | 3 means 23). Team Red’s leaves are on the left and Team Blue’s leaves are on the right.
9 6 | 1 | 8
7 4 2 | 2 | 3 5 6 9
5 1 | 3 | 0 4
What is the median of Team Red’s scores?
questions.explanation: Team Red’s scores in order are 16, 19, 22, 24, 27, 31, 35, and the middle (4th) one is 24. 26 is Team Blue’s median — it comes from the wrong side of the stem.
steps: Team Red is on the left; read its leaves from the stem outwards: 16, 19, 22, 24, 27, 31, 35.
There are 7 scores, so the median is the 4th one in order.
The 4th score is 24, so the median is 24.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 26 is the median of Team Blue (the right side). Team Red’s leaves are on the LEFT of the stem.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 174 ÷ 7 ≈ 24.9 is the mean. The median is the middle value when the scores are in order.
mistakes.D: Step 2: stem 2 with leaf 4 is 24, not 42. Read the stem first, then the leaf, on both sides.

questions.prompt: Six test scores are 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 and 22. Their mean is 17. A seventh score of 38 is added. What are the new mean and median?
questions.explanation: The new total is 140, so the mean is 140 ÷ 7 = 20, and the middle of the 7 ordered scores is 18. The median does not stay at 16.5 — adding a value moves the middle position.
steps: Old total = 17 × 6 = 102, so the new total = 102 + 38 = 140.
New mean = 140 ÷ 7 = 20.
New order: 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 38. With 7 values the median is the 4th: 18.

mistakes.B: Step 3: the median does change — with 7 values it is the 4th one in order, not the old middle (15 + 18) ÷ 2.
mistakes.C: Step 2: (17 + 38) ÷ 2 averages the old mean with one score. Find the new total (102 + 38) and divide by 7.
mistakes.D: Step 2: adding a large value always pulls the mean up. Find the new total and divide by 7.

questions.prompt: The probability that a spinner lands on “prize” is 3/8. What is the probability that it does NOT land on “prize”?
questions.explanation: P(not prize) = 1 − 3/8 = 5/8, because an event and its complement add to 1. 3/8 is the chance of a prize, not the chance of no prize.
steps: “Prize” and “not prize” are complementary events, so their probabilities add to 1.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 3/8 is the probability that it DOES land on prize. Take it away from 1.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 3/5 compares prize with no prize. A probability compares with ALL the outcomes: subtract 3/8 from 1.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a probability can never be more than 1. Work out 1 − 3/8.

questions.prompt: The spinner in the diagram lands on red, blue, green or white. The probabilities of red, blue and white are shown. What is P(red or green)?
questions.explanation: P(green) = 1 − 0.65 = 0.35, and since red and green can’t happen together, P(red or green) = 0.3 + 0.35 = 0.65. 0.75 is P(not blue), which wrongly includes white.
steps: All the probabilities add to 1, so P(green) = 1 − (0.3 + 0.25 + 0.1) = 1 − 0.65 = 0.35.
Red and green are mutually exclusive, so add: P(red or green) = 0.3 + 0.35.
P(red or green) = 0.65.

mistakes.A: Step 1 only: 0.35 is P(green). Now add P(red), because red and green can’t happen together.
mistakes.B: Step 2: for “or” with events that can’t happen together, ADD the probabilities — don’t multiply them.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 1 − 0.25 is P(not blue), which also includes white. Find P(green) first, then add red.

questions.diagram_alt: A spinner drawn to scale: red 0.3, blue 0.25, white 0.1, and green marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the numbers are added. The grid shows every total. What is the probability that the total is NOT a multiple of 4?
questions.explanation: There are 9 cells with a total of 4, 8 or 12 out of 36, so P(multiple of 4) = 1/4 and P(not) = 3/4. Counting 11 totals as equally likely (8/11) is wrong because, for example, 7 can happen 6 ways but 12 only 1 way.
steps: The grid has 36 equally likely outcomes.
Multiples of 4: totals of 4 (3 cells), 8 (5 cells) and 12 (1 cell) — 9 cells, so P(multiple of 4) = 9/36 = 1/4.
P(not a multiple of 4) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 9/36 = 1/4 is the probability that the total IS a multiple of 4. Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the totals 2 to 12 are not equally likely. Count the 36 cells in the grid, not the 11 different totals.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you missed the total of 12 (6 + 6), which is also a multiple of 4. Count the 4s, the 8s and the 12.

questions.diagram_alt: A 6 by 6 grid showing the total of two dice for each of the 36 outcomes, from 2 to 12

questions.prompt: The Venn diagram shows which of 30 students play the guitar and which play the piano. How many students play the piano?
questions.explanation: The Piano circle holds 6 (piano only) plus 4 (both), so 10 students play the piano. Answering 6 forgets the students in the overlap, who also play the piano.
steps: The Piano circle has two parts: piano only (6) and the overlap, both (4).
Students who play the piano = 6 + 4 = 10.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 6 is the students who play piano but NOT guitar. Add the overlap too — they also play piano.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 4 is only the students who play both. The whole Piano circle also includes “piano only”.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 9 + 4 + 6 counts everyone in either circle. Only the Piano circle counts: piano only plus both.

questions.diagram_alt: Venn diagram for 30 students: guitar only 9, both guitar and piano 4, piano only 6, neither 11

questions.prompt:
A two-way table shows 80 students.
Year 7: has a pet 22, no pet 18.
Year 8: has a pet 26, no pet 14.
A Year 7 student is chosen at random. What is the probability that they have a pet?
questions.explanation: Only the Year 7 row counts: 22 of the 40 Year 7 students have a pet, so P = 22/40 = 11/20. Dividing by 80 would be right only if the student were chosen from everyone.
steps: “A Year 7 student is chosen” means only the Year 7 row matters.
Year 7 total: 22 + 18 = 40; of these, 22 have a pet.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you divided by all 80 students. The student is chosen from Year 7 only, so divide by the Year 7 total.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 48 is everyone with a pet. The student is chosen from Year 7, so divide by the Year 7 total.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 48/80 is the chance that ANY student has a pet. Use only the Year 7 row.

questions.prompt: In a class of 32 students, 18 like maths, 15 like science and 7 like neither, as shown in the Venn diagram. How many students like both maths and science?
questions.explanation: Only 25 students are inside the circles, but 18 + 15 = 33, so 33 − 25 = 8 students are counted twice — they like both. Answering 1 forgets to take out the 7 who like neither.
steps: Inside the circles (at least one subject): 32 − 7 = 25 students.
18 + 15 = 33 counts the students who like both twice.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 18 + 15 − 32 forgets the 7 students who like neither. Only 32 − 7 = 25 students are inside the circles.
mistakes.B: Step 1 only: 25 is the number who like at least one subject. Now compare it with 18 + 15.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 18 + 15 = 33 counts the overlap twice. Subtract the 25 students who are inside the circles.

questions.diagram_alt: Venn diagram for 32 students: circle Maths (18 students) and circle Science (15 students) overlap; 7 students are outside both circles; the regions inside the circles are marked with question marks

questions.prompt: A drawing pin is dropped 150 times. The column graph shows how it landed. What is the experimental probability that it lands point down?
questions.explanation: Point down happened 63 times in 150 trials, so the experimental probability is 63 ÷ 150 = 0.42. Dividing 63 by 87 compares the two results instead of dividing by all the trials.
steps: Read the graph: point down happened 63 times out of 87 + 63 = 150 drops.
Experimental probability = 63 ÷ 150 = 0.42.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 87 is the number of times it landed point UP. Use the point-down bar.
mistakes.B: Step 2: divide by the number of trials, 150 — not by 100.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 63 ÷ 87 compares point down with point up. Divide by the total number of drops, 150.

questions.diagram_alt: Column graph of 150 drops of a drawing pin: point up 87, point down 63

questions.prompt: Zac rolls a die and keeps a running total of the number of fives. After 30 rolls he has 8 fives, after 150 rolls he has 31 fives, and after 600 rolls he has 108 fives. Using the best estimate from his results, about how many fives would you expect in 1500 rolls?
questions.explanation: The latest running total (108 fives in 600 rolls) gives P(five) ≈ 0.18, and 0.18 × 1500 = 270. Using the first 30 rolls (400) relies on far too few trials.
steps: Running totals include all the earlier rolls, so the 600-roll figure is the most reliable.
Best estimate: P(five) ≈ 108 ÷ 600 = 0.18.
Expected fives in 1500 rolls ≈ 0.18 × 1500 = 270.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 8/30 uses only the first 30 rolls. The 600-roll total includes them and is far more reliable.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 31/150 is not the latest total. Use the biggest running total: 108 fives in 600 rolls.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 1/6 is the theory for a fair die. The question asks you to use Zac’s results.

questions.prompt: A data set has five values: 7, 8, 12, 15 and one more value, y. The mean of the five values is 11. What is the range of the data set?
questions.explanation: The total is 55, so y = 13, and the data in order is 7, 8, 12, 13, 15, giving a range of 15 − 7 = 8. Using y as the largest value (13 − 7 = 6) forgets that 15 is bigger.
steps: A mean of 11 for 5 values means the total is 11 × 5 = 55.

mistakes.A: Step 3: y = 13 is not the largest value — 15 is. Range = largest − smallest.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the total of FIVE values is 11 × 5 = 55, not 11 × 4. With the right total, y = 13 and 15 stays the largest.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 15 − 12 is the largest value minus the median. The range is largest minus smallest.
